claim: The gut microbiota communicates with the central nervous system (CNS) in a bidirectional manner thereby influencing brain function and behavior.
source: Accumulating evidence indicates that the gut microbiota communicates with the central nervous system (CNS) in a bidirectional manner thereby influencing brain function and behavior (Sampson and Mazmanian, 2015; Dinan and Cryan, 2012; Mayer, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to other scholarly work (Sampson and Mazmanian, 2015; Dinan and Cryan, 2012; Mayer, 2011).

claim: The gut microbiota may have a role in visceral pain.
source: Although the majority of studies investigating the effects of the microbiota on brain function involve animal models of anxiety, depression, and cognitive dysfunction, it is now becoming clear that the gut microbiota may also have a role in other CNS-related conditions, such as visceral pain (O'Mahony et al., 2014; Gareau et al., 2007; McKernan et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to other scholarly work (O'Mahony et al., 2014; Gareau et al., 2007; McKernan et al., 2010).

claim: Abdominal pain is often characterized by visceral hypersensitivity.
source: Abdominal pain, often characterized by visceral hypersensitivity, is a common, and at times, dominant symptom of several gastrointestinal disorders, including functional dyspepsia and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) (Enck et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to other scholarly work (Enck et al., 2016) and draws from established scientific consensus.

claim: There is a high comorbidity among visceral pain and psychiatric disorders such as depression and anxiety.
source: There is also a high comorbidity among visceral pain and psychiatric disorders such as depression and anxiety (Felice et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to other scholarly work (Felice et al., 2015).

claim: Many gastrointestinal disorders with visceral pain as a component lack an identifiable pathology and can be difficult to treat with current pharmaceuticals.
source: Moreover, many gastrointestinal disorders with visceral pain as a component lack an identifiable pathology and can be difficult to treat with current pharmaceuticals, many of which are associated with undesirable side effects (Wood, 2013; Moloney et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to other scholarly work (Wood, 2013; Moloney et al., 2016).

claim: The perception of visceral pain is a complex process involving peripheral sensory nerves, and, in the CNS, spinal and cortical pathways as well as areas associated with integration of the experience of pain.
source: The perception of visceral pain is a complex process involving peripheral sensory nerves, and, in the CNS, spinal and cortical pathways as well as areas associated with integration of the experience of pain (Apkarian et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to other scholarly work (Apkarian et al., 2005) and draws from established scientific consensus.

claim: Pathological pain states have been associated with altered neuroimmune signaling and glial activation in the spinal cord.
source: Pathological pain states have been associated with altered neuroimmune signaling and glial activation in the spinal cord (Ji et al., 2013; Grace et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to other scholarly work (Ji et al., 2013; Grace et al., 2014).

claim: There is a significant overlap in brain areas regulating the affective component of visceral pain and those mediating psychological stress.
source: In the brain, there is a significant overlap in areas regulating the affective component of visceral pain and those mediating psychological stress, a major predisposing factor for visceral hypersensitivity (Larauche et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to other scholarly work (Larauche et al., 2012).

claim: Imaging studies in humans with IBS and in animal models of visceral hypersensitivity have revealed increased activation in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) in response to both viscerally painful and stressful stimuli.
source: Imaging studies in humans with IBS (Tillisch et al., 2011; Mertz et al., 2000) and in animal models of visceral hypersensitivity (Gibney et al., 2010; Felice et al., 2014; Bliss et al., 2016) have revealed increased activation in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) in response to both viscerally painful and stressful stimuli.
evidence: Supported by citations to other scholarly work (Tillisch et al., 2011; Mertz et al., 2000; Gibney et al., 2010; Felice et al., 2014; Bliss et al., 2016).

claim: Specific bacterial strains (probiotics) have been shown to ameliorate visceral pain induced by stress or antibiotic administration in rodent studies.
source: In rodent studies, specific bacterial strains (probiotics) have been shown to ameliorate visceral pain induced by stress (Gareau et al., 2007; McKernan et al., 2010; Ait-Belgnaoui et al., 2006) or antibiotic administration (Verdú et al., 2006), and many probiotics have been shown to benefit humans with abdominal pain (Clarke et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to other scholarly work (Gareau et al., 2007; McKernan et al., 2010; Ait-Belgnaoui et al., 2006; Verdú et al., 2006; Clarke et al., 2012).

claim: Many probiotics have been shown to benefit humans with abdominal pain.
source: In rodent studies, specific bacterial strains (probiotics) have been shown to ameliorate visceral pain induced by stress (Gareau et al., 2007; McKernan et al., 2010; Ait-Belgnaoui et al., 2006) or antibiotic administration (Verdú et al., 2006), and many probiotics have been shown to benefit humans with abdominal pain (Clarke et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to other scholarly work (Clarke et al., 2012).

claim: Visceral hypersensitivity can be transferred via the microbiota of IBS patients to animals previously lacking microbes.
source: Intriguingly, visceral hypersensitivity can be transferred via the microbiota of IBS patients to animals previously lacking microbes (Crouzet et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to other scholarly work (Crouzet et al., 2013).

claim: GF mice displayed increased visceral pain responses compared to controls.
source: (A) GF mice displayed increased visceral pain responses compared to controls.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and statistical analysis (main effect of pressure: F4,60 = 76.75, p<0.001; main effect of group: F1,15 = 12.51, p=0.0030).

claim: The pain threshold was lower in GF compared to CC mice.
source: (B) The pain threshold was lower in GF compared to CC mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and statistical analysis (t17 = 2.12, p=0.049).

claim: GF mice displayed visceral hypersensitivity at pressures of 10, 40, 65, and 80 mmHg.
source: Post hoc analyses revealed that GF mice displayed visceral hypersensitivity at pressures of 10, 40, 65, and 80 mmHg (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and post hoc statistical analyses.

claim: There was no significant difference in the basal activity (between distensions) of the abdominal musculature between groups.
source: Importantly, in line with our previous studies (O'Mahony et al., 2012), there was no significant difference in the basal activity (between distensions) of the abdominal musculature between groups (F1,15 = 0.38, p=0.58) or within the same experimental group (F4,60 = 1.08, p=0.374).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis (F1,15 = 0.38, p=0.58), and citation to previous work (O'Mahony et al., 2012).

claim: In GF mice, the transcription levels of TLR1, TLR2, TLR3, TLR4, TLR5, TLR7, TLR9, and TLR12 were significantly increased in the lumbosacral spinal cord compared to controls.
source: In GF mice, the transcription levels of TLR1 (t18 = 2.92, p=0.0093), TLR2 (t17 = 2.56, p=0.020), TLR3 (t18 = 2.81, p=0.012), TLR4 (t18 = 2.38, p=0.029), TLR5 (t17 = 3.16, p<0.0057), TLR7 (t17 = 2.49, p=0.023), TLR9 (t16 = 2.22, p=0.041), and TLR12 (t13 = 2.55, p=0.024) were significantly increased in the lumbosacral spinal cord compared to controls (Figure 2A–H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A–H and statistical analyses.

claim: No changes were observed in the expression of TLR6, TLR8, and TLR11 in GF mice compared to controls.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analyses showing no significant differences.

claim: In GF mice, there was a significant increase in the transcription levels of IL6, IL10, TNFα, IL1α, and IL1β compared to CC mice.
source: In GF mice, there was also a significant increase in the transcription levels of IL6 (t17 = 2.80, p=0.012), IL10 (t17 = 2.11, p=0.050), TNFα (t17 = 2.80, p=0.0015), IL1α (t16 = 2.27, p=0.038), and IL1β (t15 = 2.74, p=0.016) compared to CC mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analyses.

claim: No changes were observed in the expression levels of IFNγ, IL12a, and IL12b in GF mice compared to CC mice.
source: However, no changes were observed in the expression levels of IFNγ (t18 = 0.31, p=0.76), IL12a (t18 = 0.30, p=0.77), and IL12b (t18 = 0.75, p=0.46; Figure 2I–P).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I–P and statistical analyses showing no significant differences.

claim: The anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) was 21% smaller in GF mice compared to controls.
source: The anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) was 21% smaller in GF mice compared to controls (t10 = 2.78, p=0.020).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis (t10 = 2.78, p=0.020).

claim: There were no significant differences in the volumes of the prelimbic (PL) and infralimbic (IL) cortices between groups.
source: There were no significant differences in the volumes of the prelimbic (PL) and infralimbic (IL) cortices between groups (PL: t10 = 0.90, p=0.39; IL: t10 = 1.56, p=0.15).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analyses showing no significant differences.

claim: Total cortical volume was not significantly different in CC and GF mice.
source: Total cortical volume was not significantly different in CC and GF mice (t9 = 0.77, p=0.46).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis (t9 = 0.77, p=0.46).

claim: The PAG was 22% larger in GF compared to CC mice.
source: The PAG was 22% larger in GF compared to CC mice (t9 = 3.83, p=0.0040).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis (t9 = 3.83, p=0.0040).

claim: There was no significant difference in the distance from the pia for neurons from CC and GF mice.
source: There was no significant difference in the distance from the pia for neurons from CC and GF mice (t8 = 0.96, p=0.36; Figure 4D), indicating that neurons from both groups were located in similar topographical locations (i.e. cell layer) in the ACC.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and statistical analysis (t8 = 0.96, p=0.36).

claim: The basilar dendrites of GF mice were 22% longer than controls.
source: The basilar dendrites of GF mice were 22% longer than controls, but there was no significant change in apical dendritic length (apical: t8 = 1.72, p=0.12; basilar: t8 = 2.65, p=0.029; Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and statistical analysis (basilar: t8 = 2.65, p=0.029).

claim: There was no significant change in apical dendritic length between GF and CC mice.
source: The basilar dendrites of GF mice were 22% longer than controls, but there was no significant change in apical dendritic length (apical: t8 = 1.72, p=0.12; basilar: t8 = 2.65, p=0.029; Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and statistical analysis (apical: t8 = 1.72, p=0.12).

claim: There was no significant group difference in the number of branch points in either apical or basilar dendrites.
source: There was no significant group difference in the number of branch points in either apical or basilar dendrites (apical: t8 = 0.73, p=0.49; basilar: t8 = 0.39, p=0.71; Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F and statistical analyses showing no significant differences.

claim: 2D Sholl analysis revealed no significant group differences in ACC pyramidal neuron total dendritic distribution.
source: 2D Sholl analysis revealed no significant group differences in ACC pyramidal neuron total dendritic distribution (main effect F1, 8 = 2.16, p=0.18; interaction F14, 112 = 1.43, p=0.15; Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G and statistical analysis.

claim: Sholl analysis revealed a significant interaction of group (CC vs GF) and distance from the soma on the distribution of apical dendrites.
source: Sholl analysis revealed a significant interaction of group (CC vs GF) and distance from the soma on the distribution of apical dendrites (F14, 112 = 3.06, p<0.001); however, post hoc comparisons uncovered no statistically significant dendritic regions in which the change in complexity occurred (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H and statistical analysis (F14, 112 = 3.06, p<0.001).

claim: There was no significant difference in the complexity of the basilar dendrites between CC and GF mice.
source: There was no significant difference in the complexity of the basilar dendrites (main effect F1, 8 = 3.29, p=0.11; interaction F14, 112 = 0.67, p=0.80; Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I and statistical analysis.

claim: There was no significant difference in spine width on any portion of the dendritic arbor between CC and GF mice.
source: There was no significant difference in spine width on any portion of the dendritic arbor (overall: t8 = 0.16, p=0.88; apical: t8 = 0.16, p=0.88; basilar: t8 = 0.16, p=0.88; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and statistical analyses showing no significant differences.

claim: There was no significant group difference in spine length overall, on apical or basilar dendrites.
source: Similarly, there was no significant group difference in spine length overall, on apical or basilar dendrites (overall: t8 = 0.23, p=0.82; apical: t8 = 0.38, p=0.72; basilar: t8 = 0.83, p=0.43; Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and statistical analyses showing no significant differences.

claim: The overall spine density was 26% higher in GF mice.
source: The overall spine density (includes all spine subtypes) was 26% higher in GF mice (t8 = 3.46, p=0.0085; Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and statistical analysis (t8 = 3.46, p=0.0085).

claim: Spine density was increased by 23% and 31% on apical and basilar dendrites, respectively, in GF mice.
source: This increase in spines occurred on all portions of the dendritic arbor: spine density was increased by 23% and 31% on apical and basilar dendrites, respectively (apical: t8 = 3.22, p=0.012; basilar: t8 = 3.11, p=0.014; Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and statistical analyses.

claim: GF mice had 20% more thin spines overall on ACC pyramidal neurons compared to controls.
source: GF mice had 20% more thin spines overall on ACC pyramidal neurons compared to controls (t8 = 2.50, p=0.037; Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G and statistical analysis (t8 = 2.50, p=0.037).

claim: There was a strong trend toward an increase in thin spines on basilar dendrites but no such effect on apical dendrites in GF mice.
source: This increase in thin spines appears to be principally located on basilar dendrites: there was a strong trend toward an increase in thin spines on basilar dendrites but no such effect on apical dendrites (apical: t8 = 1.73, p=0.13; basilar: t8 = 2.20, p=0.060; Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G and statistical analyses.

claim: In GF mice, the overall stubby spine density was increased by 53% compared to controls.
source: In GF mice, the overall stubby spine density was increased by 53% compared to controls (t8 = 3.30, p=0.011; Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H and statistical analysis (t8 = 3.30, p=0.011).

claim: The basilar dendrites of GF mice had 69% more stubby spines while there was no change in apical stubby spine density.
source: The higher stubby spine density was located to the basilar dendritic arbor: the basilar dendrites of GF mice had 69% more stubby spines while there was no change in apical stubby spine density (apical: t8 = 2.04, p=0.076; basilar: t8 = 4.77, p=0.0014; Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H and statistical analyses.

claim: There was no significant group difference in mushroom spine density on any portion of the dendritic arbor.
source: There was no significant group difference in mushroom spine density on any portion of the dendritic arbor (overall: t8 = 1.55, p=0.16; apical: t8 = 1.53, p=0.16; basilar: t8 = 1.53, p=0.16; Figure 4—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1I and statistical analyses showing no significant differences.

claim: There was no group difference in filopodia spine density overall, or on apical and basilar dendrites.
source: Finally, there was no group difference in filopodia spine density overall, or on apical and basilar dendrites (overall: CC = 0.041 ± 0.0067, GF = 0.065 ± 0.015, t8 = 1.43, p=0.19; apical: CC = 0.037 ± 0.010, GF = 0.065 ± 0.016, t8 = 1.43, p=0.19; basilar: CC = 0.044 ± 0.0051, GF = 0.065 ± 0.014, t8 = 1.33, p=0.22).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analyses showing no significant differences.

claim: Microbial colonization normalized visceral pain perception in response to colonic stimulation.
source: Microbial colonization normalized visceral pain perception in response to colonic stimulation (main effect of pressure: F4,68 = 33.42, p<0.001; main effect of group: F2,17 = 11.85, p<0.001; Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and statistical analysis.

claim: The pain threshold was normalized in GFC mice.
source: The pain threshold was also normalized in GFC mice (F2,25 = 4.56, p=0.021; Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and statistical analysis (F2,25 = 4.56, p=0.021).

claim: GFC animals displayed normalized gene expression levels of TLR1, TLR2, TLR4, TLR5, TLR7, and TLR12.
source: GFC animals displayed normalized gene expression levels of TLR1 (F2,46 = 7.35, p=0.0018), TLR2 (F2,45 = 5.77, p=0.0060), TLR4 (F2,47 = 6.05, p=0.0047), TLR5 (F2,45 = 3.98, p=0.026), TLR7 (F2,44 = 6.96, p=0.0024), and TLR12 (F2,45 = 4.64, p=0.015).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analyses.

claim: Microbial colonization normalized the expression levels of TLR3 and TLR9 in relation to CC mice, but no significant differences were observed between GFC and GF mice.
source: Although microbial colonization normalized the expression levels of TLR3 (F2,45 = 4.04, p=0.025) and TLR9 (F2,46 = 3.54, p=0.038) in relation to CC mice, no significant differences were observed between GFC and GF mice (Figure 6A–H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A–H and statistical analyses.

claim: Microbial colonization normalized the gene expression levels of IL6, TNFα, and IL10.
source: Similarly, microbial colonization normalized the gene expression levels of IL6 (F2,27 = 6.12, p=0.0068), TNFα (F2,42 = 4.38, p=0.019), and IL10 (F2,43 = 6.01, p=0.0050).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analyses.

claim: Microbial colonization normalized the expression of IL1α and IL1β compared to controls; however, there was no statistical difference between GFC and GF mice.
source: Microbial colonization normalized the expression of IL1α (F2,46 = 3.52, p=0.038) and IL1β (F2,37 = 7.10, p=0.0026) compared to controls; however, there was no statistical difference between GFC and GF mice (Figure 6I–M).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6I–M and statistical analyses.

claim: No significant changes were observed in gene expression levels of TRPV1 between groups.
source: In addition, gene expression levels of TRPV1 were measured. No significant changes were observed between groups (F2, 20 = 0.28, p=0.7621; Figure 6N).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6N and statistical analysis showing no significant differences.

claim: TLRs are predominantly expressed on astrocytes and microglia within the CNS.
source: Because TLRs are predominantly expressed on astrocytes and microglia within the CNS (Lehnardt et al., 2003), we investigated the relationship between glia and the enhanced gene expression of several TLRs in the spinal cord.
evidence: Supported by citation to other scholarly work (Lehnardt et al., 2003) and draws from established scientific consensus.

claim: Protein levels of GFAP and Cd11b were increased in the spinal cord of GF versus CC mice.
source: Similarly to TLRs, protein levels of GFAP and Cd11b, respective markers of astrocyte and glial activation (Yao et al., 2014; Bignami et al., 1972), were increased in the spinal cord of GF versus CC mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to other scholarly work (Yao et al., 2014; Bignami et al., 1972).

claim: Microbial colonization normalized the protein levels of GFAP and CD11b to control levels.
source: Importantly, microbial colonization normalized the protein levels of GFAP (F2,17 = 79.6, p<0.001; Figure 7A) and CD11b (F2,19 = 47.47, p<0.001; Figure 7B) to control levels.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and 7B and statistical analyses.

claim: Expression levels of IL6 and TNFα were significantly increased in GF mice compared to CC mice and normalized following the microbial colonization.
source: Expression levels of IL6 (F2,23 = 4.70, p=0.021, Figure 7C) and TNFα (F2,24 = 4.79, p=0.019; Figure 7D) were significantly increased in GF mice compared to CC mice and normalized following the microbial colonization.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and 7D and statistical analyses.

claim: Microbial colonization returned the protein expression of IL10 to baseline in relation to CC mice, but no significant differences were observed between GFC and GF mice.
source: Although microbial colonization returned the protein expression of IL10 to baseline in relation to CC mice (F2,23 = 3.74, p=0.041, Figure 7E), no significant differences were observed between GFC and GF mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E and statistical analysis.

claim: The values for IL1α and IL1β were below detection range.
source: The values for IL1α and IL1β were below detection range.
evidence: Supported by experimental observation.

claim: No significant differences were observed in the levels of expression of IL12 and IFNγ between groups.
source: No significant differences were observed in the levels of expression of IL12 (CC: 0.6341 ± 0.158, GF: 0.8422 ± 0.142, GFC: 0.7896 ± 0.121, F2, 21 = 0.58, p=0.57) and IFNγ (CC: 0.0141 ± 0.0038, GF: 0.1271 ± 0.0013, GFC: 0.0137 ± 0.0041, F2, 24 = 0.19, p=0.82) between groups.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analyses showing no significant differences.

claim: Mice raised in GF conditions exhibited visceral hypersensitivity and an increase in cytokine and TLR expression in the spinal cord.
source: Our results show that mice raised in GF conditions exhibited visceral hypersensitivity and an increase in cytokine and TLR expression in the spinal cord.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from multiple experiments showing visceral hypersensitivity and increased cytokine and TLR expression.

claim: Postnatal microbial colonization normalizes the visceral hypersensitivity and spinal cord inflammatory profile of GF mice.
source: We have also demonstrated that postnatal microbial colonization normalizes the visceral hypersensitivity and spinal cord inflammatory profile of GF mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing normalization of visceral hypersensitivity and inflammatory markers after colonization.

claim: GF mice had increased ACC and decreased PAG volumes as well as dendritic hypertrophy of single pyramidal neurons in the ACC.
source: In addition, we found that these animals had increased ACC and decreased PAG volumes as well as dendritic hypertrophy of single pyramidal neurons in the ACC.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing volumetric changes and dendritic morphology alterations.

claim: The gut microbiota is required for normal visceral nociception and pain processing at the level of the CNS.
source: Taken together, these results clearly indicate that the gut microbiota is required for normal visceral nociception and pain processing at the level of the CNS.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results showing altered pain responses and CNS changes in GF mice.

claim: Exposure to stressors or antibiotic treatment in early life can have enduring effects on visceral pain in rodents, and these effects are accompanied by a change in microbial composition.
source: We have previously shown that exposure to stressors or antibiotic treatment in early life can have enduring effects on visceral pain in rodents, and these effects are accompanied by a change in microbial composition (O'Mahony et al., 2014, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (O'Mahony et al., 2014, 2009).

claim: Probiotics can exert an inhibitory influence on visceral sensitivity in healthy rats.
source: Moreover, in rodents, probiotics can ameliorate visceral pain induced by stress (Gareau et al., 2007; McKernan et al., 2010; Ait-Belgnaoui et al., 2006) or antibiotic administration (Verdú et al., 2006), and even exert an inhibitory influence on visceral sensitivity in healthy rats (Kamiya et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to other scholarly work (Kamiya et al., 2006).

claim: The composition of the gut microbiota is altered in patients with IBS.
source: Clinical studies have repeatedly found that the composition of the gut microbiota is altered in patients with IBS (Collins, 2014; Jeffery et al., 2012) and that patients suffering from abdominal pain can benefit from probiotic treatment (Clarke et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to other scholarly work (Collins, 2014; Jeffery et al., 2012).

claim: Patients suffering from abdominal pain can benefit from probiotic treatment.
source: Clinical studies have repeatedly found that the composition of the gut microbiota is altered in patients with IBS (Collins, 2014; Jeffery et al., 2012) and that patients suffering from abdominal pain can benefit from probiotic treatment (Clarke et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to other scholarly work (Clarke et al., 2012).

claim: The exact mechanism by which the microbiota exerts its influence on the CNS remains unknown.
source: Although it is now clear that the gut microbiota plays a role in visceral nociception, the exact mechanism by which the microbiota exerts its influence on the CNS remains unknown.
evidence: Acknowledged gap in knowledge based on current understanding.

claim: Many systems simultaneously contribute to the altered nociception in GF mice, including immune, neural, endocrine, and metabolic processes.
source: It is likely that many systems simultaneously contribute to the altered nociception in GF mice, including immune, neural, endocrine, and metabolic processes (Sampson and Mazmanian, 2015; Dinan and Cryan, 2012; Mayer, 2011; Luczynski et al., 2016; Cryan and Dinan, 2012).
evidence: Speculative statement supported by citations to other scholarly work (Sampson and Mazmanian, 2015; Dinan and Cryan, 2012; Mayer, 2011; Luczynski et al., 2016; Cryan and Dinan, 2012).

claim: GF mice have blunted immune function and altered TLR expression in the gut.
source: Indeed, GF mice have blunted immune function and altered TLR expression in the gut (Shanahan, 2002; Clarke et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to other scholarly work (Shanahan, 2002; Clarke et al., 2013).

claim: The development in early life and function of the enteric nervous system (ENS) in adulthood is altered in GF mice.
source: Interestingly, the development in early life and function of the enteric nervous system (ENS) in adulthood is altered in GF mice (Collins et al., 2014; McVey Neufeld et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to other scholarly work (Collins et al., 2014; McVey Neufeld et al., 2013).

claim: Enteric sensory neurons synapse with vagal nerve endings in the gut, providing a direct route whereby the intestinal bacterial status can be communicated to the brain.
source: Enteric sensory neurons synapse with vagal nerve endings in the gut (Perez-Burgos et al., 2014), providing a direct route whereby the intestinal bacterial status can be communicated to the brain.
evidence: Supported by citation to other scholarly work (Perez-Burgos et al., 2014) and draws from established scientific consensus.

claim: Growing up germ-free heightens hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis responsivity, which is thought to occur via a neuronal mechanism.
source: Growing up germ-free heightens hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis responsivity, which is thought to occur via a neuronal mechanism (Sudo et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to other scholarly work (Sudo et al., 2004).

claim: GF rodents have a reduced production of short chain fatty acids.
source: GF rodents also have a reduced production of short chain fatty acids (den Besten et al., 2013), which are metabolites produced by gut bacteria thought to be key mediators of gut-brain signaling.
evidence: Supported by citation to other scholarly work (den Besten et al., 2013).

claim: Short chain fatty acids are metabolites produced by gut bacteria thought to be key mediators of gut-brain signaling.
source: GF rodents also have a reduced production of short chain fatty acids (den Besten et al., 2013), which are metabolites produced by gut bacteria thought to be key mediators of gut-brain signaling.
evidence: Draws from established scientific consensus and citation (den Besten et al., 2013).

claim: Nociceptors in the gastrointestinal tract respond to many stimuli including stretch, pH, bacterial products, immune signaling molecules, and neurotransmitters released from the ENS or from the bacteria themselves.
source: Within the gastrointestinal tract, nociceptors respond to many stimuli including stretch, pH, bacterial products, immune signaling molecules, and neurotransmitters released from the ENS or from the bacteria themselves (Sengupta, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to other scholarly work (Sengupta, 2009) and draws from established scientific consensus.

claim: Recent evidence has implicated neuroimmune and spinal microglial mechanisms in chronic visceral pain.
source: Recent evidence has implicated neuroimmune and spinal microglial mechanisms in chronic visceral pain (Ji et al., 2013; Grace et al., 2014; Bradesi, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to other scholarly work (Ji et al., 2013; Grace et al., 2014; Bradesi, 2010).

claim: TLR receptor signaling is involved in visceral nociception and IBS pathology.
source: TLR receptor signaling is also involved in visceral nociception and IBS pathology (Tramullas et al., 2014, Tramullas et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to other scholarly work (Tramullas et al., 2014, Tramullas et al., 2016).

claim: Microglial structure and homeostasis are disrupted in both GF and antibiotic-treated mice.
source: Moreover, microglial structure and homeostasis are disrupted in both GF and antibiotic-treated mice (Erny et al., 2015), indicating that the microbiota is required for normal microglial function in the CNS.
evidence: Supported by citation to other scholarly work (Erny et al., 2015).

claim: The microbiota is required for normal microglial function in the CNS.
source: Moreover, microglial structure and homeostasis are disrupted in both GF and antibiotic-treated mice (Erny et al., 2015), indicating that the microbiota is required for normal microglial function in the CNS.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that microglial structure and homeostasis are disrupted in GF and antibiotic-treated mice, supported by citation (Erny et al., 2015).

claim: Microglia can be activated through TLR signaling, and once activated, increase the secretion of various cytokines.
source: Microglia can be activated through TLR signaling, and once activated, increase the secretion of various cytokines (Bradesi, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to other scholarly work (Bradesi, 2010) and draws from established scientific consensus.

claim: Microglial activation, reduced glutamate-reuptake by astrocytes, and increased TLR signaling in the spinal cord have been previously shown in rodent models with visceral hypersensitivity.
source: Indeed, microglial activation (Saab et al., 2006), reduced glutamate-reuptake by astrocytes (Gosselin et al., 2010), and increased TLR signaling (Tramullas et al., 2014) in the spinal cord have been previously shown in rodent models with visceral hypersensitivity.
evidence: Supported by citations to other scholarly work (Saab et al., 2006; Gosselin et al., 2010; Tramullas et al., 2014).

claim: TRPV1 receptors are broadly expressed in the gastrointestinal tract and many areas of the CNS, including the spinal cord and is well-recognized as a transducer of noxious stimuli.
source: TRPV1 receptors are broadly expressed in the gastrointestinal tract and many areas of the CNS, including the spinal cord and is well-recognized as a transducer of noxious stimuli (Nagy et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to other scholarly work (Nagy et al., 2004) and draws from established scientific consensus.

claim: The colon of GF mice exhibits the same responsiveness to capsaicin (a TRPV1 agonist) relative to controls.
source: This result is in line with previous data from our group showing that the colon of GF mice exhibits the same responsiveness to capsaicin (a TRPV1 agonist) relative to controls (Lomasney et al., 2014), suggesting no change in the expression of the TRPV1 receptor.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Lomasney et al., 2014).

claim: Rats exposed to vancomycin early in life resulting in an altered gut microbiome show enhanced visceral pain perception and a decrease in spinal cord TRPV1 expression.
source: In contrast, rats exposed to vancomycin in early in life resulting in an altered gut microbiome, show enhanced visceral pain perception and a decrease in spinal cord TRPV1 expression (O'Mahony et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to other scholarly work (O'Mahony et al., 2014).

claim: TRPV1 receptors play a key role in pain perception in the gut.
source: In the gut, TRPV1 receptors play a key role in pain perception (Holzer, 2011); however, TRPV1 signaling does not appear to be responsible for the visceral hypersensitivity observed in GF mice.
evidence: Supported by citation to other scholarly work (Holzer, 2011) and draws from established scientific consensus.

claim: TRPV1 signaling does not appear to be responsible for the visceral hypersensitivity observed in GF mice.
source: In the gut, TRPV1 receptors play a key role in pain perception (Holzer, 2011); however, TRPV1 signaling does not appear to be responsible for the visceral hypersensitivity observed in GF mice.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing no change in TRPV1 expression in GF mice.

claim: The affective or emotional component of pain is mediated by the ACC.
source: The affective or emotional component of pain is mediated by the ACC (Apkarian et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to other scholarly work (Apkarian et al., 2005) and draws from established scientific consensus.

claim: Imaging studies have consistently observed reduced cortical grey matter in patients with IBS.
source: In addition, imaging studies have consistently observed reduced cortical grey matter in patients with IBS (Davis et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to other scholarly work (Davis et al., 2008).

claim: Rodents with long-lasting neuropathic pain show a reduction of ACC volume.
source: Although cortical structure has yet to be investigated in animal models of visceral pain, rodents with long-lasting neuropathic pain show a reduction of ACC volume (Seminowicz et al., 2009) and basilar dendritic hypertrophy of pyramidal neurons (Metz et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to other scholarly work (Seminowicz et al., 2009).

claim: Rodents with long-lasting neuropathic pain show basilar dendritic hypertrophy of pyramidal neurons.
source: Although cortical structure has yet to be investigated in animal models of visceral pain, rodents with long-lasting neuropathic pain show a reduction of ACC volume (Seminowicz et al., 2009) and basilar dendritic hypertrophy of pyramidal neurons (Metz et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to other scholarly work (Metz et al., 2009).

claim: GF mice showed no difference in mushroom spines, which represent mature, long-lasting postsynaptic connections.
source: Importantly, GF mice showed no difference in mushroom spines, which represent mature, long-lasting postsynaptic connections (Matsuzaki et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to other scholarly work (Matsuzaki et al., 2004).

claim: The density of 'immature' thin and stubby spines was higher in GF mice.
source: Instead, the density of 'immature' thin and stubby spines was higher in these animals.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing increased thin and stubby spine density.

claim: Changes in ACC signaling would likely impact visceral sensitivity, as this area receives and sends projections to many pain-relevant brain areas including the limbic system, ventral tegmental area and the PAG.
source: Such changes in ACC signaling would likely impact visceral sensitivity, as this area receives and sends projections to many pain-relevant brain areas including the limbic system, ventral tegmental area and the PAG (Hoover and Vertes, 2007).
evidence: Speculative statement supported by citation to other scholarly work (Hoover and Vertes, 2007) and draws from established scientific consensus.

claim: The neurons in the PAG, once activated are involved in an endogenous pain inhibitory system.
source: The neurons in the PAG, once activated are involved in an endogenous pain inhibitory system (Apkarian et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to other scholarly work (Apkarian et al., 2011) and draws from established scientific consensus.

claim: The PAG receives signals from cortical areas such as the ACC where this connection is thought to mediate expectation and placebo analgesia.
source: The PAG receives signals from cortical areas such as the ACC where this connection is thought to mediate expectation and placebo analgesia (Petrovic et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to other scholarly work (Petrovic et al., 2002) and draws from established scientific consensus.

claim: Gross morphological and ultrastructural changes in the ACC and PAG could underlie the visceral hypersensitivity observed in GF mice.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that gross morphological and ultrastructural changes in the ACC and PAG could underlie the visceral hypersensitivity observed in GF mice.
evidence: Speculative statement inferred from the experimental results showing morphological changes and visceral hypersensitivity.

claim: The microbial composition of mice in conventional facilities may affect the responsiveness to CRD.
source: These results further reinforce the idea that the microbial composition of mice in conventional facilities may affect the responsiveness to CRD (Verdú et al., 2006).
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results and supported by citation to other scholarly work (Verdú et al., 2006).

claim: This maladaptive pain responsivity is amenable to microbial-based interventions in later life.
source: Importantly, this maladaptive pain responsivity is amenable to microbial-based interventions in later life.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing normalization of pain responses after microbial colonization.

claim: Certain behavioral and physiological changes in GF mice prove reversible with postnatal colonization.
source: This is noteworthy as numerous postnatal colonization experiments have been performed in GF mice, with certain behavioral and physiological changes proving reversible (Clarke et al., 2013; Sudo et al., 2004; Diaz Heijtz et al., 2011) and others irreversible (Desbonnet et al., 2014; Stilling et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to other scholarly work (Clarke et al., 2013; Sudo et al., 2004; Diaz Heijtz et al., 2011).

claim: Certain behavioral and physiological changes in GF mice prove irreversible with postnatal colonization.
source: This is noteworthy as numerous postnatal colonization experiments have been performed in GF mice, with certain behavioral and physiological changes proving reversible (Clarke et al., 2013; Sudo et al., 2004; Diaz Heijtz et al., 2011) and others irreversible (Desbonnet et al., 2014; Stilling et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to other scholarly work (Desbonnet et al., 2014; Stilling et al., 2015).

claim: The effects of the microbiome on brain and behaviour are much more robust in males than females.
source: Moreover, we find across a number of different domains that the effects of the microbiome on brain and behavioural are much more robust in males than females (Clarke et al., 2013; Desbonnet et al., 2015; Hoban et al., 2016).

claim: Improving our understanding of the impact of microbiota on visceral pain sensitivity may ultimately inform novel therapies for the treatment of gastrointestinal pain disorders.
source: Improving our understanding of the impact of microbiota on visceral pain sensitivity (O'Mahony et al., 2017) may ultimately inform novel therapies for the treatment of gastrointestinal pain disorders.
evidence: Speculative statement about future implications, supported by citation (O'Mahony et al., 2017).
